paragraphs: Gloucestershire County Council runs its own not-for-profit fostering service and says it usually turns to its own carers first when a local child needs a home. Children in its care may also live with independent agencies such as those listed on this page.

The council says it particularly needs carers for long-term homes for children over five, for brothers and sisters who need to stay together (which means more than one spare room), for children over 10 and teenagers, for short breaks for children over 10 (at least two weekends a month), and for children with disabilities or additional needs.

Its recruitment page asks for applicants aged over 21 with a spare room, some experience of caring for children (any children of your own need to be over two), time to give a child stability, a driving licence and basic IT skills. You can be single, married, divorced or cohabiting for at least two years, and you can rent or own, work or not. Non-British citizens need indefinite leave to remain.

The council advertises weekly fees of £122.50 to £331.59 per child, depending on experience and the type of fostering, on top of age-related maintenance allowances. Training is held in the county, and carers have their own social worker, a separate social worker for the child, specialist mental health support, out-of-hours help and a local carers' community.
Before you decide, compare what the council offers with two or three of the agencies below, and ask each about training, support and placements in your part of the county.
